deepDive.title: The Dancing Marquess: Anglesey's Butterfly in Diamonds
deepDive.answerFirst: Henry Cyril Paget, 5th Marquess of Anglesey (1875–1905), converted the chapel of Plas Newydd on Anglesey into a 150-seat theatre, spent a fortune on jewels and costumes, performed a snake-like "Butterfly Dance," and died bankrupt at 29 — his family then erasing him from history.
deepDive.html:
Come up the Menai Strait to Plas Newydd and you are standing where Britain's most flamboyant aristocrat blazed a path of burning torches to light his guests up to his private theatre. This is the house of Henry Cyril Paget — "Toppy" to the few who loved him, the "Dancing Marquess" to the press, and "the black sheep" to a family that spent decades pretending he had never existed.

He was born in Paris in 1875, amid whispers — recorded by his own biographers — that his true father was the French actor Benoît-Constant Coquelin rather than the 4th Marquess. Fostered in France until he was eight, he arrived on Anglesey a solitary, theatrical boy in a house of hunting men. When his father died in November 1898, the 23-year-old inherited the marquessate, some 30,000 acres, and an annual income of roughly £110,000 — a river of money he would drain in six extraordinary years.

Paget renamed the ancestral seat "Anglesey Castle" and did the thing his descendants could never forgive: he took the family chapel and turned it into the Gaiety Theatre, a 150-seat auditorium fitted, by 1901, with electric stage lighting. Here, opulently costumed, he took the lead in everything from pantomime to Shakespeare's Henry V to Oscar Wilde's An Ideal Husband — a pointed choice, since Wilde had been jailed for "gross indecency" only in 1897. He hired professional actors down from Llandudno, and staged free performances for servants, tradesmen, students and neighbours.

His signature turn made his name. Borrowing from the American dancer Loïe Fuller, he performed what the press dubbed the Butterfly Dance: swathed in a voluminous robe of transparent white silk, waved under coloured electric light like wings. Contemporaries described "sinuous, sexy, snake-like dances." Between the acts he handed out photographic postcards of himself in costume.

Then there were the jewels. Paget bought them by the fistful, sewing real diamonds onto stage costumes, keeping a Pekingese in pink ribbons, and — most gloriously — modifying his car's exhaust to spray perfume in its wake. His marriage, in January 1898, to his cousin Lilian Florence Maud Chetwynd, was later annulled — on the grounds of non-consummation. One persistent story, repeated in the costume he supposedly draped his cousin in nightly with jewels before returning them to the vault, points to a marriage that was pageant rather than partnership.

The reckoning came fast. On 11 June 1904 he was declared bankrupt, with debts of £544,000 — jewellers heading the creditor list — a sum variously reckoned at £50–70 million today. The "Great Anglesey Sale" dispersed his treasures; it was said he even sold his housekeeper's parrot, reputedly able to swear in several languages. He died in Monte Carlo on 14 March 1905, just short of thirty, his ex-wife at his side. One obituary judged: "From boyhood to death no one had ever loved him."

What his cousin did next is the second scandal. Succeeding as 6th Marquess, Charles Henry Alexander Paget destroyed all the 5th Marquess's papers and reconverted the Gaiety Theatre back into a chapel. Queer history, as the modern stage biographer Seiriol Davies puts it, is erased. The Paget debts helped force the sale of the family's English seat at Beaudesert in the 1930s.

Why did the family try to erase the Dancing Marquess?

Because he embodied everything Edwardian aristocracy feared: extravagance, effeminacy, theatricality and possible queerness. His successor burned his records and dismantled his theatre; artefacts were sold or lost in the 1904 sale. Only recently have the National Trust, exhibitions at Plas Newydd, the musical How to Win Against History and the 2024 film Madfabulous restored him.

Was the Dancing Marquess gay?

He is claimed today as an icon of queer and gender-nonconforming heritage — the National Portrait Gallery, PinkNews and the Historic queer-places project all treat him so. The documented facts are his cross-dressing performances, his jewellery and furs, and his annulled, unconsummated marriage. Beyond that, direct evidence was largely destroyed by his family, so his precise private life remains, honestly, undocumented.

What survives at Plas Newydd today?

The house and gardens are National Trust and open to the public. The chapel-turned-theatre-turned-chapel survives within the house; the Trust displays photographs of the 5th Marquess in costume and, since 2018, a dedicated room with a reproduction costume and a mock-up of the Gaiety. The lower terraces and Gothic Hall doors feature in Madfabulous.

  • Who: Henry Cyril Paget, 5th Marquess of Anglesey (1875–1905)
  • Where: Plas Newydd, Llanfairpwllgwyngyll, Anglesey (National Trust)
  • Claim to fame: the Gaiety Theatre; the Butterfly Dance; £544,000 bankruptcy (11 June 1904)
  • Buried: St Edwen's Church, Llanedwen
  • Access: NT house & garden, seasonal opening; check winter closures

deepDive.title: Ffynnon Elian: The Cursing Well of North Wales
deepDive.answerFirst: Ffynnon Elian at Llanelian-yn-Rhos, Conwy, was North Wales's most feared "cursing well." From about 1743 to 1850, for a fee you could write an enemy's name on slate, drop it in the water, and invoke St Elian's wrath. The well was destroyed around 1850.
deepDive.html:
Most holy wells in Wales heal. This one killed — or so thousands believed. Ffynnon Elian, on the farmland above Llanelian-yn-Rhos near Colwyn Bay, began life as an ordinary healing well, where pilgrims paid a groat, or its value in bread, and tried three times to empty the water to cure a sick child. But from roughly 1743 the well acquired a far darker trade, and became the most notorious cursing well in the Principality.

The mechanism was chillingly simple, and it is described in Francis Jones's The Holy Wells of Wales and by the antiquarian Thomas Pennant, who wrote of it in his History of Whiteford and Holywell (1796). You went to the keeper of the well. Your enemy's name was written on parchment or scratched on a slate and dropped into the water; sometimes a wax effigy was made and stuck with pins. Passages were read from the Bible or Apocrypha; the well-water was given to you thrice, to drink and to pour over your head. For your fee — a shilling or more — the victim would be afflicted with illness, ruin or death. For a higher fee, the keeper could lift a curse. Pennant records that whole farms were said to have been cursed at the well; he himself was once threatened with "the vengeance of St Elian."

This was not merely the superstition of the poor. The last keeper claimed his clients included "the best people in the land in terms of wealth and education," from England and Ireland too. A Nonconformist minister who believed himself cursed at the well took to his bed and became seriously ill. The trade was lucrative — one custodian reputedly earned up to £300 a year.

The most famous keeper was John Evans, "Jac Ffynnon Elian." He inherited the business, elaborated its rituals, and was twice gaoled — for fraud, for charging to lift curses that had never been cast — before finally, publicly, admitting the whole thing was bogus. The local Methodist minister and congregation set out to destroy the well around 1828–29; Jac diverted the water onto his own land to keep trading, but the well was finally choked up and destroyed around 1850. Even then belief lingered: in the 1860s a visitor to the remains found corks stuck with pins floating in the water, and an 1870 commentator confirmed "the ill fame of Ffynnon Elian continues even to this day." An 1925 excavation reportedly recovered a small slate with a wax effigy pinned to it, cursing one "R.F."

Where is the cursing well now, and can you visit it?

The well site lies on private farmland (Cefn-y-ffynnon) north of Llanelian-yn-Rhos village; Coflein records it as filled in, with a cobbled path remaining. There is no public access to the well itself. The visitable, photographable site is the medieval church of St Elian a few hundred yards away.

Was the cursing real, or a con?

The belief was entirely real and had real effects — people sickened from terror. The mechanism was a paid ritual run by keepers, the last of whom (Jac Ffynnon Elian) confessed to fraud. Historians (Richard Suggett, A History of Witchcraft and Magic in Wales; Thomas Waters, Yale) treat it as documented folk magic and social history.

What can I photograph at Llanelian-yn-Rhos?

St Elian's Church — with its remarkable late-medieval painted rood-screen panels (dendro-dated to timber felled 1498–1528) — and the historic White Lion Inn beside the churchyard, in continuous use since roughly the church's own age.

  • Where: Ffynnon Elian, Llanelian-yn-Rhos, Conwy (grid SH86077692)
  • Cursing phase: c.1743–1850
  • Last keeper: John Evans, "Jac Ffynnon Elian" (jailed for fraud)
  • Access: well on PRIVATE land, no access; St Elian's Church visitable
  • Sources: Thomas Pennant (1796); Francis Jones, Holy Wells of Wales

PHOTOGRAPHY NOTE: The well itself is on private farmland with no public access — do NOT attempt to reach it; photograph St Elian's Church (open, with medieval painted panels) and the White Lion Inn instead. A footpath runs near the well site. RCAHMW holds a Crown-copyright church exterior image (not free-licence). Best visual: the church interior rood-screen panels and the churchyard with the inn sign.

deepDive.title: The Maid of Buttermere: A Beauty, a Bigamist and a Hanging
deepDive.answerFirst: Mary Robinson, the "Maid of Buttermere," was the Fish Inn landlord's beautiful daughter who in 1802 was tricked into a bigamous marriage by John Hatfield, an impostor posing as "Colonel Hope." Coleridge exposed him in the Morning Post; Hatfield was hanged at Carlisle in 1803.
deepDive.html:
Walk into Buttermere today and the Fish Inn still stands — the very inn where, in 1792, a passing travel-writer named Joseph Budworth "discovered" a fifteen-year-old girl with, he wrote, "lips as red as vermilion" and cheeks with "more of the lily than the rose." He put her in his guidebook A Fortnight's Ramble to the Lakes as a tourist attraction, and so began the strange public life of Mary Robinson, the Maid of Buttermere.

For a decade she was a sight to tick off — a beauty the Lakeland tourists came to gawp at, praised by Wordsworth, the Coleridges and the Lambs alike. Then, in the summer of 1802, into this remote valley drove a handsome gentleman in a fine travelling carriage, calling himself the Honourable Colonel Alexander Augustus Hope, MP for Linlithgow, brother of the Earl of Hopetoun. He courted Mary with polished manners and forged letters of credit, and on 2 October 1802 they married at Lorton church.

It was a sham built on sand. The groom's real name was John Hatfield — an undischarged bankrupt, serial impostor and forger, who had already abandoned wives and children and served years in gaol for debt. And here is the delicious twist of literary history: the marriage was reported in the London papers through the Keswick correspondent of the Morning Post — none other than Samuel Taylor Coleridge, who deemed the union of "the Beauty of Buttermere" and a brother of an earl a "Romantic Marriage." That report, dated 11 October 1802, reached people in Scotland who knew the real Colonel Hope was abroad. By 6 November the London Sun had unmasked the impostor.

Hatfield, "if nothing else a smooth operator," borrowed money and fled — to Ravenglass to hide on a ship, then via Chester into Wales, where the Bow Street Runners took him near Swansea. He was tried at Carlisle not for bigamy but for forgery — a capital offence — and hanged at the Sands in Carlisle on 3 September 1803. Reports dwell on his composure: he reputedly corrected the rope himself when the hangman fumbled.

And Mary? She had been left pregnant; the child was stillborn in 1803. But the nation's sympathy was total. Wordsworth, who had known her, wrote her into The Prelude as one "unspoiled by commendation and the excess of public notice." She married a Caldbeck farmer, Richard Harrison, in 1807, had four children, and is buried in St Kentigern's churchyard at Caldbeck — the same churchyard, incidentally, that holds the huntsman John Peel. In 1987 Melvyn Bragg turned the whole affair into his novel The Maid of Buttermere.

Was the Maid of Buttermere a real person?

Yes — Mary Robinson (1778–1837) was entirely real, the daughter of the Fish Inn's landlord at Buttermere. Her beauty, the 1802 bigamous marriage to John Hatfield, and his execution are all documented in contemporary newspapers, Wordsworth's The Prelude, and the Oxford Dictionary of National Biography.

What was John Hatfield's real crime?

He was hanged for forgery (specifically franking letters as an MP and passing forged bills), which was a capital offence in 1803 — not, technically, for the bigamy that made him infamous. He was already married when he wed Mary.

What survives at Buttermere today?

The Fish Inn (now the Bridge/Fish Hotel) still trades in Buttermere village and marks Mary's story; a plaque commemorates her. Lorton church (where she married) and St Kentigern's, Caldbeck (where she is buried) both survive and are visitable.

  • Who: Mary Robinson (1778–1837); John Hatfield (c.1758–1803)
  • Where: Fish Inn, Buttermere; Lorton church; Caldbeck churchyard
  • When: married 2 Oct 1802; Hatfield hanged 3 Sep 1803
  • Chronicler: S. T. Coleridge, Morning Post; Wordsworth, The Prelude
  • Access: Fish Inn open (pub/hotel); churches freely visitable

PHOTOGRAPHY NOTE: The Fish Inn at Buttermere is a working pub/hotel — freely photographable from the road and lakeside; ask before interior shots. Combine with Buttermere lake itself (National Trust valley) for golden-hour reflections. Lorton church and St Kentigern's, Caldbeck, are open churches with free access and parking. Strongest visual: the Fish Inn with the Buttermere fells behind. A public-domain Gillray-after engraving of "Mary of Buttermere" exists via the British Museum.

background: Around Paradise Street, Wapping and Park Lane, Liverpool's nineteenth-century Sailortown served one of the world's busiest ports. Period authorities counted hundreds of brothels and thousands of women working in or around the sailors' quarter, although all such estimates are necessarily uncertain. The district also ran on crimping: lodging-house keepers and agents controlled sailors' wages, credit and access to ships. Contemporary and later accounts often sensationalised this trade, so the evidence needs the same correction applied to Tiger Bay: exploitation was real, but a working migrant district was more than the respectable city's story about it.

background: Blackpool's railways, wakes weeks and Golden Mile made it the great working-class seaside resort. Its presiding comic form was the saucy postcard, and its best-known artist was Donald McGill, credited with thousands of designs and an enormous print circulation. In July 1954, aged seventy-nine, McGill pleaded guilty at Lincoln under the Obscene Publications Act 1857 and was fined. The episode joins Blackpool's popular humour to Holywell Street's obscenity-law story: inexpensive, visible pleasure drew attention that private and expensive forms often escaped.

background: The Contagious Diseases Acts of 1864, 1866 and 1869 applied to designated garrison and port districts including Aldershot. Police could identify a woman as a common prostitute and subject her to repeated internal examination; infection could mean confinement in a lock hospital. No matching regime examined or detained the servicemen whose health the legislation claimed to protect. Josephine Butler and the Ladies' National Association turned opposition into a major campaign against the sexual double standard. The Acts were suspended in 1883 and repealed in 1886.

background: The Cam near Grantchester acquired Byron's name from the tradition that he swam here while at Trinity. A century later the place entered the Bloomsbury orbit: Rupert Brooke and Virginia Stephen are recorded bathing naked by moonlight in 1911. The site is now a Local Nature Reserve, so the literary associations should not be mistaken for an invitation to ignore current access, water or conservation guidance.

hook: Highgate Men's Pond turned a former reservoir into one of London's longest-lived single-sex outdoor swimming spaces, where public bodies and private sociability have long met.

sources.publisher: City of London, Hampstead Heath swimming

background: Hampstead Heath's ponds began as water-company reservoirs and became democratic swimming places. The men's pond was formally opened for swimming in 1893 and remains in use. Its social history includes privacy, bodily freedom and queer community, but it is first of all a living public facility: present-day opening, safety and admission information should be checked with the City of London.

hot_spot_stories.title: The winter swimmers
hot_spot_stories.body: The pond's cold-water swimmers became a press fascination and later defended year-round access. Their story belongs to bodily freedom and community rather than erotic spectacle—a distinction this map should keep clear.

sources.publisher: City of London, Hampstead Heath swimming

background: Opened to the public in 1926, the ladies' pond is an enduring women-only natural swimming place. Its history encompasses changing ideas of bodily visibility, community and who may claim space outdoors. Claims that it is unique in Europe should be treated cautiously unless tied to a current authoritative source; its documented longevity is distinctive enough.

hook: Hampstead's Mixed Pond records the slow normalisation of men and women swimming together in open water after Victorian resorts had regulated even their proximity.

background: The Heath's reservoir ponds became swimming waters during the nineteenth century. The mixed pond offers a useful counterpoint to Llandudno's former segregation rules: a shared outdoor space in which mixed bathing became ordinary. It remains an operating facility, and its present rules, water conditions and seasonal access matter more to a visit than the historical map pin.

hook: The Serpentine placed outdoor swimming in the ceremonial centre of London, turning public bathing and the visible body into part of everyday metropolitan life.

sources.publisher: The Royal Parks, swimming in the Serpentine
The Royal Parks, Hyde Park history timeline

background: Hyde Park's Serpentine has a long association with bathing and organised swimming, including the Serpentine Swimming Club. Its relevance here is not that swimming is inherently erotic, but that access to uncovered bodies in public was repeatedly negotiated through rules of class, gender, propriety and safety. Contemporary swimming is confined to designated arrangements, so historic custom is not current access advice.
